nameStory: The white-lipped snail gets its name from the distinctive white or cream-colored rim around the opening of its shell, called the aperture. This white 'lip' is like nature's signature on each shell, making it easy to distinguish from its close cousin, the brown-lipped snail. The term 'garden banded snail' refers to both its love of garden habitats and the colorful bands that often spiral around its shell.
description: The white-lipped snail is a chunky, air-breathing land snail that you might spot crawling across your garden path on a dewy morning. These terrestrial snails carry beautiful rounded shells that can display amazing variety in color and pattern - from solid yellow or pink to striped with dark bands. They're one of the larger snails you'll encounter in New England, with shells that can reach about an inch across. Like all land snails, they're gastropods, meaning 'stomach-foot,' because they literally crawl on their bellies.

idTips.label: White shell lip
idTips.description: The shell opening has a distinctive white or cream-colored rim that feels smooth to the touch - this is the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Variable shell colors
idTips.description: Shells range from bright yellow to pink, brown, or white, often with dark spiral bands - the diversity is remarkable even within the same population

idTips.label: Rounded shell shape
idTips.description: Shell feels solid and globe-shaped when held, wider than it is tall, with a low spire that doesn't stick up much

idTips.label: Smooth shell texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels glossy and smooth when clean, with fine growth lines you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Active crawler
idTips.description: Often seen gliding smoothly across surfaces, leaving a silvery mucus trail that feels slightly sticky

habitat: White-lipped snails thrive in gardens, parks, and woodland edges throughout New England, especially where there's plenty of calcium in the soil for shell-building. Look for them in areas with some moisture - under logs, in leaf litter, around stone walls, and in well-established gardens with rich, alkaline soil. They particularly love areas where wild ginger, ferns, and other shade-loving plants create a cool, humid microclimate.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm, often seen crawling on wet mornings after spring rains. This is prime time for spotting them as they emerge from winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid weather and after rainstorms, but may retreat during hot, dry periods. Look for them in the early morning when dew provides moisture.
seasonality.fall: Remain active through early fall, often more visible as they feed heavily before winter. Shell colors may appear more vibrant in the crisp autumn light.
seasonality.winter: Seal themselves into their shells with a temporary door and hibernate under logs, leaves, or in soil crevices. Empty shells are sometimes found after harsh weather.

funFact: These snails are living mood rings - the incredible variety of colors and patterns in their shells is partly determined by their diet and temperature during shell growth, meaning siblings from the same clutch of eggs can end up looking completely different from each other!
confusionNotes: The brown-lipped snail looks nearly identical except for its dark brown or black shell lip instead of white. Memory trick: 'White-lipped = white rim, brown-lipped = brown rim' - it's really that simple! The shell patterns and colors can be identical between the two species, so always check that lip color.
contextualKnowledge: These snails are actually non-native to North America, originally from Europe, but they've been here so long they're considered naturalized. Don't confuse the 'garden' in their alternate name with being garden pests - while they do nibble plants occasionally, they're more likely to be cleaning up decaying matter and are generally harmless to healthy gardens.
compareHints: The white-lipped snail is virtually identical to the brown-lipped snail in size, shape, and shell patterns, but the lip color is the dead giveaway - white versus dark brown or black. Both species often live in the same areas and have the same lifestyle, making the lip color the only reliable way to tell them apart. Other New England land snails are typically much smaller or have more elongated, pointed shells.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Brown-lipped snails differ from white-lipped snails primarily in that distinctive lip color around the shell opening - brown versus white or pale.
